Ramp MCP connects AI tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor to your Ramp account. Each connection acts as the signed-in user, with that user's Ramp permissions.

```
claude mcp add --transport http ramp https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
```

```
codex mcp add ramp --url https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
```

* **Other clients:** Coding agents can also use Ramp CLI. For other MCP clients, gateways, and the sandbox, see Connect to Ramp.

When you sign in, choose **Full access** or **Read-only**. Connections expire after 30 days; reconnect to renew.

Developer Docs

# **Ramp MCP**

---

Ramp MCP connects AI tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor to your Ramp account. Each connection acts as the signed-in user, with that user's Ramp permissions.

## Connect

* **Claude:** Install Ramp from Claude's directory, then sign in to Ramp.
* **ChatGPT:** Install Ramp from the ChatGPT app directory.
* **Cursor:** Add Ramp to Cursor with one click.
* **Claude Code:**

```
claude mcp add --transport http ramp https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
```

  

* **Codex:**

```
codex mcp add ramp --url https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp
```

  

* **Other clients:** Coding agents can also use Ramp CLI. For other MCP clients, gateways, and the sandbox, see Connect to Ramp.

When you sign in, choose **Full access** or **Read-only**. Connections expire after 30 days; reconnect to renew.

Ramp MCP connects Ramp to AI tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor. From those tools, you can review spend, look up bills and vendors, and handle approvals and expenses. A connected tool can only see and do what your Ramp role allows, and Ramp attributes its actions to you.

* Claude: Install Ramp from Claude's MCP directory, then sign in to Ramp.
* ChatGPT: Install Ramp from the ChatGPT app directory.
* Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor: Connect with Ramp MCP or the Ramp CLI. See Connect Ramp to an agent.
* Other AI tools: Any tool that supports remote MCP servers with OAuth can connect to

| Area | Try asking |
| --- | --- |
| Spend analysis | "Show me our top software vendors by spend this quarter." |
| Bills | "Find our open bills from AWS and when they're due." |
| Approvals | "Summarize the bills and reimbursements waiting on my approval and flag anything unusual." |
| Expenses | "Find my draft lunch reimbursement from Tuesday and tell me what is missing." |
| Receipts and memos | "Which of my transactions from the last 14 days are missing receipts or memos?" |
| Receipt upload | "Upload the receipt for my Uber ride last Tuesday." |
| Policy and help | "Is my planned $300 client dinner within policy?" |
| Cards and funds | "Lock my card — I can't find it." |
| Procurement | "Submit a procurement request for 20 Figma seats." |
| Travel | "Show my upcoming flights and hotels for next month." |
| Ramp Banking | "Get all Ramp Banking account balances for today's cash snapshot." |

> Important: If you're an approver, the AI tool can approve or reject transactions, reimbursements, bills, and requests on your behalf. Approving a bill can send it to payment.

* Coding agents, the Ramp CLI, and custom MCP clients: See the Ramp agent docs.
* Custom clients and MCP gateways such as Glean, MintMCP, or Microsoft Copilot Studio: Ramp must allowlist the redirect URI first. Submit a redirect URI allowlist request.
* Custom integrations: Use the Ramp Developer API.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard developed by Anthropic that enables applications to expose data and functionality to LLMs. MCP provides an LLM with access to pretty much anything you want: databases, your computer’s filesystem, Figma, GitHub, etc. Given that Ramp’s developer API is the primary way to access Ramp’s resources externally, we wanted to see what would happen if we put the two together.

An MCP server in Python can be built using `FastMCP`. MCP "tools" are akin to HTTP endpoints the LLM can access through an MCP client. The following piece of code, for example, is reminiscent of a `Flask` HTTP endpoint decorated with `@app.route(…)` and OpenAPI spec schemas.

Using `FastMCP` and a lightweight Ramp developer API client, we were able to build a working early prototype of the Ramp MCP server. With Claude Desktop as our MCP client, Claude was able to both generate visualizations and run simple analyses on spend data pulled from Ramp’s APIs using natural language. Adding a new source of data *— like a different API endpoint —* was as simple as defining a new tool. As a proof of concept, we had it issue cards on demand for a company offsite.

Our initial setup worked fine on a small demo business, but we quickly ran into a few scaling issues: miscalculations, limited context windows, input size limits, and high input token usage. At first we hacked together a simple pagination tool to chunk responses into smaller, digestible parts, but we struggled to scale meaningfully beyond a few hundred transactions. Then we asked Claude what it would prefer the data to look like, and it said it preferred predictable data formats that enabled server-side functions. That sounded like SQL: structured, predictable, and built for querying. Most importantly, Claude could now load as little raw data into its context window as possible, making the server do most of the heavy computational lifting. Thanks to the reduced token usage in this approach, Ramp MCP now even worked with the free version of Claude.

MCP and similar technologies can introduce information security risk if left unchecked. LLMs can pull and understand large amounts of data from any source at their disposal. This means authentication credentials like API keys need to be secured, and following the principle of least privilege is as crucial as ever. As a mitigant, we implemented audit logging and you can pick a constrained set of OAuth scopes and tools to make available to the MCP client.
